summary: Describes Quality for Service (Q4S), an application-level protocol based on HTTP and SDP for communicating end-to-end quality compliance. It negotiates and monitors latency, jitter, bandwidth and packet loss, and raises alerts when negotiated conditions are violated.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a video call, two sides check the connection is good enough and keep an eye on it, shouting if it gets worse.

subtitle: Application-level protocol for monitoring end-to-end quality of service

tldr.problem: Applications that need real-time communication (video calls, online gaming) struggle to know whether network quality is good enough, and cannot react to degradation.
tldr.mechanism: Q4S runs alongside the application and continuously measures latency, jitter, bandwidth, and packet loss using test messages. It alerts both sides when these metrics drop below agreed thresholds.
tldr.outcome: Applications can adapt their behavior when quality degrades, and network operators can make informed decisions about quality constraints. Q4S is an informational protocol without IETF standard status.

today: RFC 8802 is an Informational RFC describing Q4S as research work without IETF consensus. It provides a foundation for quality measurement in real-time applications but has not been adopted as a standard protocol. Implementations would need to build Q4S stacks that run alongside application protocols.

sections.title: The Problem Q4S Solves
sections.content:
Real-time applications like video conferencing and online gaming need network connections to meet certain quality standards. Quality of Service (QoS) is measured by four key metrics: latency (how fast messages arrive), jitter (how much latency varies), bandwidth (how much data per second), and packet loss (percentage of data that fails to arrive).

Q4S is an application-level protocol that lets two endpoints negotiate, measure, and monitor these four metrics end-to-end. Unlike older quality measurement systems, Q4S is designed to run in parallel with application traffic and help applications react in real time when quality drops below what was agreed upon.
sections.plainLanguage: Q4S is like checking the road conditions before and during a trip to make sure you can get there on time.

sections.title: How Q4S Works
sections.content:
Q4S follows a client-server model with four distinct phases. The Handshake phase begins when a client sends a BEGIN request to the server, proposing quality requirements in SDP (Session Description Protocol) format. The server responds with its actual requirements for the session.

The Negotiation phase has two stages. Stage 0 measures latency and jitter using PING requests sent bidirectionally between client and server. Stage 1 measures bandwidth and packet loss using BWIDTH messages. If measurements meet the agreed constraints, both sides can proceed; if not, the server sends a Q4S-ALERT and measurements repeat.

Once constraints are met, the Continuity phase begins and the application can start. Q4S continues sending periodic PING messages to monitor quality and alert if thresholds are violated. The Termination phase occurs when the client sends a CANCEL message.
sections.plainLanguage: Q4S checks if the connection is good (Handshake), makes sure it stays good (Negotiation), watches it while you work (Continuity), then cleans up when you're done (Termination).

sections.title: Q4S Messages and Methods
sections.content:
Q4S defines seven methods for communication, each serving a specific purpose. BEGIN starts a quality session and can include an SDP body with proposed quality parameters. READY signals readiness to move between negotiation stages (READY 0, 1, or 2). PING measures round-trip latency and jitter; responses are always returned. BWIDTH measures bandwidth and packet loss without requiring responses.

Three methods handle alerts and recovery. Q4S-ALERT notifies that quality constraints have been violated. Q4S-RECOVERY indicates that quality has improved after a period of degradation. CANCEL terminates the session. All messages use a format similar to HTTP, with a request line, headers, and an optional SDP body.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message type tells one side what the other side is doing: starting the check (BEGIN), moving to the next step (READY), checking the line (PING), checking bandwidth (BWIDTH), warning about problems (ALERT), saying it's better (RECOVERY), or stopping (CANCEL).

sections.title: Two Ways to Handle Quality Problems
sections.content:
Q4S supports two alerting modes for different network scenarios. In the Q4S-aware-network mode, the server sends Q4S-ALERT messages directly to the client. Network elements along the path can inspect these alerts and adjust their behavior. This mode works when the infrastructure itself is Q4S-aware.

In the Reactive mode (the default), the server sends alert notifications to an Actuator, a separate entity responsible for decision-making. The Actuator decides whether to notify the application to adapt (reduce video quality, for example) or to contact a network policy server to request better connectivity. This separation allows the same Q4S measurements to trigger different reactions depending on the application's needs and network operator's policies.
sections.plainLanguage: When quality drops, Q4S can warn the network directly (Q4S-aware mode) or tell a helper that decides what to do (Reactive mode).

sections.title: Security and Deployment Notes
sections.content:
Q4S raises several security concerns that applications must address. Measurement data could be intercepted to learn about application requirements or network topology. Authentication and encryption via HTTPS or TLS are recommended to protect the control messages. Measurement data itself should be authenticated to prevent attackers from injecting false quality information.

Q4S can be abused by sending large numbers of BWIDTH messages to consume bandwidth, or by sending Q4S-ALERT messages to trigger unnecessary application adaptation. Networks deploying Q4S should implement rate limiting and validate that alerts are legitimate.

The protocol is designed to coexist with other quality measurement systems like OWAMP and TWAMP, but serves a different purpose: OWAMP and TWAMP measure network delay only, while Q4S measures application-relevant metrics and supports reactive adaptation.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad actors could trick Q4S into thinking quality is bad when it is not, or use the measurement messages as a weapon. Networks need to verify the messages are real and limit how fast they can arrive.
